Consult Summary:
- Acute headache in a 26-year-old woman with photophobia, nausea, neck stiffness, and a history suggestive of migraine; management planned with stronger analgesia and migraine-focused follow-up.

History:
- Presenting complaint: Headache ongoing for about 3 days, primarily around the right eye, described as dull most of the time with episodic sharpness; intensity about 8/10.
- Timeline: Symptoms began ~3 days ago at work, progressively worsening; by the next day it was worse and present most days with fluctuations in intensity.
- Exacerbating/relieving factors: Light worsens pain (photophobia); ibuprofen used with little relief over the past 2 days.
- Associated symptoms: Photophobia (light hurts eyes), nausea/sick feeling without vomiting, neck stiffness; no focal weakness, no speech difficulty, no vision loss reported; difficulty focusing at work.
- Allergies: None known.
- Past medical history: History of headaches; no prior migraine diagnosis reported. Family history positive for migraines (mother and sister). Regular medications: none.
- Social history: Lives with three housemates; works in IT (high screen time, stress related to new project). Social smoker and social drinker.
- Eye history: Wears glasses since age 5; no recent eye exam documented.
- Menstrual/contraception: Not discussed beyond “on the pill” question being asked; patient reported not taking regular meds.
- Review of systems: No fever, no rashes, no vision loss; neck stiffness noted.

Past Medical History:
- Headaches (unspecified type in the past). No prior migraine diagnosis documented.
- Family history: Migraines in mother and sister.
- No chronic illnesses or other medical conditions documented.
- Allergies: None known.
- Medications: None regularly; recent ibuprofen use described below.

Medications:
- Ibuprofen: three tablets per day for two days; route not documented; dose per tablet not documented; duration ~2 days; currently no relief.
- No regular medications listed.
- Allergies: None known.

Social History:
- Occupation: IT professional; high screen time; recent project-related stress.
- Living situation: Four (including patient) in household.
- Smoking: Social smoker.
- Alcohol: Social drinker.

Family History:
- Migraines in mother and sister (mother reportedly more symptomatic; sister less so).

Physical Examination:
- Vitals: Not recorded.
- Examination findings: Not recorded.
- Neuro/eye exam: Not documented in transcript.

Investigations:
- No tests or imaging mentioned or ordered.

Assessment & Plan:
- Overall Impression:
  - Working diagnosis: Acute migraine headache (likely migraine without aura) given unilateral/right-eye-dominant pain, photophobia, nausea, gradual onset over 3 days, and positive family history. The clinician notes a migraine-like presentation and discusses treatment options accordingly.
- DDx Integration (brief):
  - Migraine (without aura) with possible genetic predisposition
    - Supporting: unilateral/right-eye predominance, photophobia, nausea, 3-day progressive course, family history.
    - Opposing: No documented aura, no vomiting, no prior formal migraine diagnosis.
  - Tension-type headache
    - Supporting: stress/work-related factors, high screen time, dull diffuse pain.
    - Opposing: Photophobia and nausea more typical of migraine.
  - Meningitis/encephalitis (less likely)
    - Supporting: neck stiffness, photophobia.
    - Opposing: No fever, no altered mental status, no rapid progression.
  - Medication-overuse headache (MOH) (possible consideration)
    - Supporting: NSAID use (three tablets/day) for 2 days; ongoing pain prompting stronger analgesia.
    - Opposing: MOH typically requires longer-term overuse.
  - Conflict noted: none.
- Issue 1: Acute migraine headache
  - Summary: Acute migraine-type headache suspected; limited relief with NSAIDs; family history supports migraine.
  - Plan:
    - Consider stronger analgesia (e.g., Naproxen) and/or combination analgesics (paracetamol ± codeine) as discussed.
    - Prescription provided for stronger relief today.
    - Continue NSAID use with appropriate dosing guidance; review dosing if needed.
    - Keep a daily headache diary to identify triggers and patterns.
    - Follow-up in 1 week to 2 weeks; reassess need for migraine prophylaxis if headaches become more frequent.
    - Safety net: return sooner if symptoms worsen, if there is vision loss, focal weakness, confusion, fever, or neck stiffness progresses.
- Issue 2: Photophobia and neck stiffness with persistent headache
  - Summary: Photophobia and neck stiffness present; no focal deficits documented.
  - Plan:
    - Monitor symptoms; if neck stiffness worsens or new neurological signs appear, reassess promptly.
    - No immediate imaging unless red flags develop (e.g., fever, altered mental status, focal deficits).
- Issue 3: Lifestyle and trigger management
  - Summary: Headache may be related to work stress, dehydration, and screen exposure.
  - Plan:
    - Hydration: ensure adequate fluid intake.
    - Screen/environment: reduce brightness, take screen breaks, ergonomic adjustments.
    - Stress management: consider workload adjustments, relaxation strategies.
General plan items:
- Education on red flags and when to seek urgent care.
- Schedule follow-up in 1–2 weeks; sooner if symptoms escalate.

Quality Checks:
- Missing but clinically expected elements: Vitals and a focused neurological/ophthalmologic exam not recorded; no explicit imaging or lab data ordered. Documented assessment relies on history; physical exam not available in transcript.
- Conflicts between transcript and DDx: None identified; DDx aligns with the clinician’s impression in the transcript.
- Transcript quality: Dialogue is somewhat informal and repetitive but provides essential history for diagnosis and plan.

Document Quality:
- Allergies: Noted as none known.
- Medications: Ibuprofen documented with partial dosing; route and per-tablet dose not documented; frequency listed as three tablets/day.
- Vitals/Exam: Not recorded.
- Investigations: None performed or ordered.

Notes: All information reflects the transcript; no external data added. If clinical course deviates or new findings emerge (e.g., fever, AMS, new focal deficits), reevaluation and possible escalation (imaging, neurology referral) would be appropriate.
